extracted.intended_audience: nonprofit staff, grant writers, and fundraisers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical post‑rejection guidance for nonprofit grantseekers on how to contact funders, what questions to ask, how to find alternative funders, and how to improve future proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express appreciation when contacting the funder
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing you want to do in your email is express your appreciation. Add a note of gratitude for considering your grant proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an individual emailed you, respond directly to them. If you only received an automated response, find a contact (use an existing relationship, Candid’s Foundation Directory, or the funder’s website contact email). Lead with gratitude before asking follow‑up questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask “Do you think I should apply again?”
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask the funder whether they recommend reapplying to understand where to best spend your time and energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This question helps reveal whether your proposal was outside the funder’s focus, or simply lost to limited funds despite being strong. If reapplication is plausible, use the opportunity to build a relationship so you’re top of mind next cycle. Suggested tactics: connect with decision‑makers on LinkedIn, personalize all communications, engage genuinely with their content, and attend conferences or funder‑hosted events (check funder calendars/newsletters for events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask “Was there something I did wrong in my proposal?”
rubrics_metrics.description: Request feedback on whether formatting or substantive issues caused the rejection so you can refine your proposal writing skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals can be rejected for small issues (wrong font) or major ones (not making a compelling argument). Specifically ask funders where your proposal missed the mark. To preempt common problems, consult resources like Candid’s blog on “7 red flags for funders,” on‑demand courses, and real‑world examples of successful proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask “Do you have any suggestions for where else I might apply?”
rubrics_metrics.description: Request recommendations for other grantmakers who might be a better fit for your project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders often network with each other and may know organizations better suited to your work, or may even make a personal introduction. If the funder has no suggestions, use tools such as Candid’s Foundation Directory and Philanthropy News Digest’s RFP Bulletin to identify aligned funders and active RFPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact method depends on how rejection was communicated
rubrics_metrics.description: How you reach out after a rejection depends on whether you received a personal email or an automated response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you received a personal message, reply directly to that person. If you only received an automated response, locate an appropriate contact via an existing relationship, the Foundation Directory, or the funder’s website contact address. Persistence in finding the right person increases chances of receiving feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and maintain relationships with decision‑makers
rubrics_metrics.description: Building relationships with funders and decision‑makers increases future funding chances and makes feedback more likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical relationship tactics: personalize communications, connect on LinkedIn, meaningfully interact with funder content, attend conferences and funder events (many organizations list public events on their websites/newsletters), and cultivate ongoing contact so you’re remembered in the next grant cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Candid tools and learning resources to find funders and improve proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage Candid’s resources to research funders and strengthen future proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundation Directory: research aligned funders, view in‑depth profiles and actual grants made. RFP Bulletin: free service publishing RFPs for U.S.‑based funders. Candid Learning: on‑demand courses and examples of successful proposals to model structure and content. Consult the “7 red flags” guidance to avoid common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you can’t get advice from the funder, apply general lessons anyway
rubrics_metrics.description: When funders won’t or can’t give feedback, still use the rejection as an opportunity to improve and seek other funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Takeaway actions: continue building relationships with decision‑makers, identify similar or better‑fitting funders to apply to, and use available learning resources to level up your grant writing for the next submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reasons proposals get rejected (diagnostic cues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical causes include misalignment with funder’s focus areas, insufficient available funds, formatting errors, or failing to make a compelling argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list as a diagnostic when reviewing your rejected proposal. Investigate whether the cause was external (scope or funding limits) versus internal (presentation, argumentation). Consult Candid’s “7 red flags” for detailed common issues and remedies.
